cls: Herbal/dietary supplement - topical emollient and oral anthraquinone stimulant laxative
pharm: Inner-leaf gel acts as a wound-healing emollient/demulcent; leaf latex (aloin/anthraquinones) acts as a colonic stimulant laxative
quick: Laxative (latex): 10-30 mg hydroxyanthracenes (as aloin) once at night; gel: topically as needed
Laxative taken at bedtime with adequate fluids; topical not applicable
Avoid oral use in significant liver disease
Serum potassium/electrolytes with chronic oral laxative use
summary: Aloe vera (Aloe barbadensis) is a botanical with two very different products. The inner-leaf gel is used topically as an emollient/wound-healing agent for minor burns, wounds, abrasions and sunburn, with limited supportive evidence. The leaf latex (yellow exudate containing anthraquinones, chiefly aloin) is a stimulant laxative for short-term relief of occasional constipation; the European HMPC dose is 10-30 mg of hydroxyanthracenes calculated as anhydrous aloin once at night, at the smallest dose producing a soft stool. Aloe is not an FDA-approved drug, and the FDA removed aloe stimulant laxatives from the US over-the-counter market in 2002 because mutagenicity/carcinogenicity safety data were not submitted. The oral laxative is contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation, intestinal obstruction, inflammatory bowel disease and children under 12, and chronic use causes potassium and electrolyte loss.
indications: Topical inner-leaf gel: minor burns (first to second degree), minor wounds, abrasions, sunburn and skin moisturizing (supportive/limited evidence)
Oral leaf latex: short-term use for occasional constipation (EMA HMPC herbal indication)

dosage.d: Herbal preparation equivalent to 10-30 mg hydroxyanthracene derivatives (as anhydrous aloin) once daily
dosage.n: Use the smallest dose producing a soft-formed stool; not for more than 1-2 weeks without medical advice

dosage.d: Apply inner-leaf gel to the affected skin as needed

admin: Take the oral laxative at night with adequate fluid intake; effect appears the next morning
Use the laxative only short-term (not more than 1-2 weeks without medical supervision)
Apply topical gel to clean, affected skin only
Avoid chronic oral laxative use, which causes dependence and electrolyte loss
Distinguish purified decolorized gel/drinks (low aloin) from the purgative latex
Monitor serum potassium if used repeatedly
moa: The two aloe products act by different mechanisms. The leaf latex contains aloin (barbaloin), a hydroxyanthracene glycoside that is a prodrug; colonic bacteria cleave it to active anthrones (e.g. aloe-emodin) that stimulate colonic motility and peristalsis and increase intestinal fluid and electrolyte secretion while reducing reabsorption, producing laxation. The inner-leaf gel contains polysaccharides (acemannan/mucopolysaccharides), amino acids and zinc; applied topically it moisturizes, is anti-inflammatory, promotes fibroblast and collagen activity and tissue regeneration, and has mild antimicrobial effects.

absolute: Intestinal obstruction or stenosis, atony (oral laxative)
Acute inflammatory intestinal disease (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis), appendicitis (oral laxative)
Abdominal pain of unknown origin (oral laxative)
Severe dehydration with electrolyte depletion (oral laxative)
Children under 12 years, pregnancy and lactation (oral laxative); hypersensitivity to aloe
relative: Significant liver disease (oral aloe associated with hepatotoxicity reports)
Conditions worsened by potassium loss (cardiac disease, concurrent diuretics/digoxin)
monitor: Serum potassium and electrolytes with chronic oral use

preg: The oral aloe laxative is contraindicated in pregnancy (EMA HMPC). Anthraquinone metabolites and theoretical stimulant/uterine concerns make oral use inappropriate. Topical gel has insufficient data but is generally regarded as low risk on intact skin, without specific endorsement.
lact: The oral laxative is contraindicated during breastfeeding because anthraquinone/anthranoid metabolites pass into breast milk and may cause infant diarrhea. Topical use is not specifically endorsed.
renal: No formal renal dose adjustment. Chronic oral laxative use causes potassium and electrolyte loss; use caution where electrolyte disturbance could worsen renal or cardiac status.
hepatic: No formal hepatic dose adjustment. Oral aloe (whole-leaf/latex) has been associated with case reports of hepatotoxicity; avoid oral use in significant liver disease.

major: Cardiac glycosides (digoxin) - hypokalemia from chronic laxative use potentiates glycoside toxicity and arrhythmia
moderate: Thiazide/loop diuretics, corticosteroids, licorice root - additive potassium loss
Antiarrhythmic and QT-affecting drugs - hypokalemia may enhance their effect
interactions.food: Oral laxative taken at night with adequate fluid, generally independent of meals.
interactions.alcohol: No specific clinically significant interaction documented.
interactions.diagnostics: Chronic use can lower serum potassium and cause melanosis coli seen at colonoscopy.

serious: Fluid and electrolyte loss, especially hypokalemia (chronic oral use)
rare: Melanosis coli (benign colonic pigmentation with chronic use)
Theoretical genotoxicity/carcinogenicity concern (basis for FDA OTC removal)
emergency: Severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from overuse

monitoring: Serum potassium and electrolytes with prolonged or repeated oral laxative use
Bowel habit and signs of laxative dependence
counsel: Use the oral laxative only for short-term, occasional constipation - not every day
Drink plenty of fluids; stop and see a doctor if you have ongoing abdominal pain
Long-term use can cause dependence and low potassium; tell your doctor if you take heart or water pills
Do not use the oral laxative if pregnant, breastfeeding, or in children under 12
The skin gel and the oral laxative are different products - use as directed
pk: Oral laxative effect typically 6-12 hours (requires colonic bacterial activation)
Acts locally in the colon; no conventional plasma peak characterized
No conventional systemic plasma half-life (local colonic action)
Single overnight dose produces a morning bowel movement
Protect from light and moisture; refrigerate natural/preservative-free topical gel after opening
pearls: NOT FDA-approved as a drug; the FDA Final Rule (2002) removed aloe stimulant laxatives from the US OTC market because requested safety (mutagenicity/carcinogenicity) data were not submitted
Distinguish the harmless emollient GEL from the purgative LATEX (aloin/anthraquinones)
Oral laxative is for short-term occasional constipation only - chronic use causes hypokalemia, dependence and melanosis coli
Hypokalemia from chronic use can potentiate digoxin and antiarrhythmics
IARC classifies whole-leaf aloe vera extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B)
missed: The oral laxative is taken only as needed for occasional constipation; if a dose is missed, simply take the next dose when needed rather than doubling up. Do not use it daily on a fixed schedule.
overdose: Overdose of the oral laxative causes watery diarrhea, severe abdominal cramps, dehydration and potassium/electrolyte depletion, which can affect the heart and neuromuscular function. Manage with fluid and electrolyte replacement and discontinue the product.
